c.tagline: Amber Coast capital of Victorian streets, cable cars, and golden beaches.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are unmetered — agree the fare before getting in, and expect fixed tourist rates from the airport and resorts. Uber operates but coverage is limited; cheap shared guaguas and motoconchos handle short local hops.

emergency.note: 911 is the Dominican Republic's unified emergency line for police, fire, and ambulance.

hood_landmark.Centro Histórico: Puerto Plata Malecon Glorieta Parque Central
hood_landmark.Playa Dorada: Playa Dorada beach resort Puerto Plata

avoid.reason: Avoid the poorer inland barrios away from the Malecón and isolated beaches after dark; stay in tourist and resort zones at night.
Watch for motoconcho overcharging, persistent street hustlers on the Malecón, and pickpockets in the Umbrella Street crowds.

hood_desc: The Victorian-era heart of the city, with its gingerbread-trimmed houses, the seafront Malecón and Glorieta bandstand on Parque Central, Fortaleza San Felipe, and the base station of the Teleférico cable car; best for travelers who want history, sights, and city life over a resort bubble.

A self-contained gated resort complex just east of the city with a golf course and a cluster of large all-inclusive hotels fronting a golden-sand beach; the easy, everything-on-site choice for a beach holiday.
A laid-back beach-and-expat residential community just west of town, with low-rise villas, condos, and a calm swimming beach; popular with long-stay visitors wanting a quiet base.
A lively beach town east along the Amber Coast built around a horseshoe bay famous for snorkeling and diving, with a compact strip (El Batey) of restaurants, bars, and nightlife.
The Dominican watersports capital farther east, a windsurfing and kitesurfing mecca with a long beach lined by beachfront bars, cafes, and a young international crowd.

water.note: Drink bottled water only, as throughout the Dominican Republic.

transit.hours: Guaguas and taxis run roughly from early morning (around 6:00 AM) to mid-evening; nightlife areas rely on taxis and motoconchos after dark.
transit.note: Puerto Plata has no metro or rail; getting around means shared guaguas (minibuses) along the coastal road, taxis, and motoconchos (motorcycle taxis), plus the tourist Teleférico cable car up Mount Isabel de Torres.
transit.pay: Guaguas and motoconchos are paid in cash (Dominican pesos) to the driver; fares are low but fixed by route, so ask the going rate before boarding.

bus: Caribe Tours and Metro coaches to Santiago and Santo Domingo
Local guaguas along the Amber Coast to Sosúa and Cabarete

transit.m: Taxi from the airport to the Malecón / city center (25-35 min)
Guagua (local minibus) along the coastal road toward town (slower, with transfers)

tip.r: A 10% service charge plus taxes is usually added to restaurant bills; leaving an extra 5-10% for good service is customary, and tipping resort staff is appreciated.
